Low-rank adapters at small ranks

By Ada Lovelace · 14 March 2025 · 9 min read

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) freezes the pretrained weights and learns a pair of thin matrices whose product is added to each adapted layer. The original paper reported that very small ranks were enough, and a year of replications has mostly agreed with it.

In this post we look at why rank 8 so often matches rank 64 on instruction tuning, and where the claim breaks down. The short answer is that the update a fine-tune needs is itself close to low rank, so extra rank mostly learns noise.

Experimental setup

We fine-tuned a 7B decoder on 52k instructions for three epochs with a cosine schedule. Every run used the same seed set, the same data order and a learning rate tuned separately for each rank, because a fixed rate quietly favours one rank over another.

RankTrainable paramsMMLUMT-Bench
42.1M45.95.81
84.2M46.86.02
6433.6M46.96.05

Why small ranks are enough

The singular values of the full fine-tuning update decay quickly: the top eight directions carry most of the energy. A rank-8 adapter can represent those directions exactly, and the remainder sits below the noise floor of a three-epoch run.

The intrinsic rank of the adaptation is low even when the model is large.

The configuration we used is short enough to show in full:

config = LoraConfig(
    r=8,
    lora_alpha=16,
    target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj"],
)

Where it breaks down

  • Continued pretraining on a new domain needs far more rank than instruction tuning.
  • Very long fine-tunes slowly use the extra capacity, so rank 64 pulls ahead after ten epochs.
  • Math-heavy data benefits from adapting the MLP blocks, not only attention.

For most instruction-tuning work, start at rank 8 and spend the saved memory on a larger batch. See the PEFT library for a reference implementation.
